extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys/agents, USPTO OED staff, and attorneys facing reciprocal discipline
extracted.subtask_description: Application of 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 to determine whether to impose identical reciprocal discipline based on a state disciplinary adjudication (Selling v. Raciford standard). It evaluates due process, infirmity of proof, grave injustice, and related finality/publication issues under a clear-and-convincing-evidence standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal-discipline presumption (Selling v. Raciford)
rubrics_metrics.description: A state disciplinary adjudication (e.g., disbarment or suspension) creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of identical reciprocal discipline is proper under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 unless the respondent meets one of the enumerated Selling elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO follows Selling v. Raciford; the presumption stands unless the respondent clearly and convincingly demonstrates a genuine issue of material fact under the listed defenses. Federal courts and the USPTO apply a narrow standard and do not sit as courts of review to reweigh evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent must prove by clear and convincing evidence that one of the defenses in 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1) applies (due process deprivation, infirmity of proof, grave injustice, or the public-discipline/finality issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a demanding showing. Case law (e.g., In re Kramer; In re Friedman; In re Zdravkovich) holds the respondent bears the burden and that the Director's review is narrow. Mere disagreement with the state court's findings is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process deprivation (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard (Mathews v. Eldridge). In disciplinary contexts this includes reasonable notice of charges, opportunity to present evidence, testify, call and cross-examine witnesses, and make arguments. Participation in hearings, representation by counsel, and the ability to present evidence generally satisfy due process. The inability to subpoena a complaining witness or normal settlement negotiations do not automatically establish deprivation of due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether there was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept the state's final conclusion on that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a difficult showing. Consent to the state findings undermines an infirmity claim. Private civil settlements (including provisions requiring withdrawal of a grievance) do not bind bar counsel and do not by themselves create an infirmity of proof. Relevant state case law (cited in the decision) indicates settlements or withdrawal by a complainant will not necessarily preclude disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether imposition of identical public censure, reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a 'grave injustice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis focuses on proportionality—whether the punishment 'fits' the misconduct. Consider the applicable range of penalties under the state rules, whether the sanction is within that range, and whether the sanction is so ill-fitted that reciprocal discipline would be unjust. Prior decisions (cited) show that sanctions within the normal range are not 'grave injustice.' State guidance (e.g., Florida Rules for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions) may inform whether the length/severity is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity/finality argument (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended, or disciplinarily disqualified (i.e., challenges based on the nature/publication or finality of the state discipline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner may attempt to argue that the state action was not a public sanction or was otherwise not final; to prevent reciprocal discipline the practitioner must show by clear and convincing evidence a genuine issue of material fact on this ground. The Decision treats such procedural/finality claims narrowly and requires substantial proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review — not a full rehearing of state proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director's review is narrow; the Director is not sitting as a court of review to discover error in the state court's or hearing judge's proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited precedent emphasizes deference to the state adjudication. The Office looks for narrow, clear-and-convincing showings of due process deprivation, infirmity, or grave injustice rather than re-litigating factual determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent to state discipline and effect on defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner's consent to a state stipulated resolution or consent judgment (including admissions or specific findings) weakens or precludes claims that the state proceeding suffered infirmity of proof or was unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the respondent expressly consented to findings of fact and discipline, those admissions are highly probative and make it difficult to satisfy the Selling defenses by clear and convincing evidence. Lack of an appeal from the state discipline further undermines respondent's challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative implementation and ancillary enforcement measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedial steps and administrative effects the Office may impose when imposing reciprocal discipline (publication and operational restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Decision orders publication in the Official Gazette and notice to state disciplinary agencies and courts where respondent is admitted; directs dissociation of respondent's name from any USPTO Customer Numbers and removal of associated PKI certificate; and bars the respondent from obtaining or being added to a USPTO Customer Number until reinstated to practice before the USPTO. These are typical ancillary enforcement measures following reciprocal discipline.
